replacement.title: Redevelopment

context.source_line: Original practice article based on the verified 2019 HKDSE Paper 4 Set 1.1 scenario (not official text):
context.title: Redevelopment: Questions and Trade-offs
body: New railway stations and private investment can quickly change an older district. Better transport may bring visitors, jobs and safer buildings, while new cafés and shops can make an area feel more lively. Owners may also welcome the chance to repair properties that have been neglected for years.

The same changes can be painful for long-term residents. When rents rise, small family businesses may close and tenants may be forced to move. Bars and restaurants can create noise late at night, and a neighbourhood may lose the services, relationships and character that once made it feel like home.

Redevelopment therefore needs more than new buildings. Residents could be consulted fairly and transparently before plans are approved, while affordable housing, compensation and support for traditional shops could reduce disruption. The central question is how Hong Kong can improve old districts without treating the people who already live there as an obstacle.

part_a.instruction: Your class is discussing the redevelopment of older districts in Hong Kong. Your group has been asked to discuss the problems redevelopment causes. You may want to talk about:

discussion_points.text: Why old districts are redeveloped
What problems redevelopments cause
What the government should do to reduce the problems residents face
anything else you think is important

part_b.instruction: The examiner will ask you one or more questions based on Part A. You will have up to 1 minute to respond.

questions.text: What do you like about the area you live in?
What is the biggest advantage of redevelopment?
What types of shops are typical of old neighbourhoods?
Why do older people like to live in traditional districts?
What would you like to change about your district?
Would you prefer to live in an old neighbourhood or a redeveloped area?
Is the redevelopment of old areas too slow in Hong Kong?
Who benefits most from redevelopment?

replacement.title: Wedding Photography

context.source_line: Original practice article based on the verified 2019 HKDSE Paper 4 Set 1.2 scenario (not official text):
context.title: Wedding Photography: Questions and Trade-offs
body: Wedding photographs are expected to preserve an important day, but couples now have many styles to choose from. Creative photographs use unusual ideas, glamorous shoots depend on impressive locations, storytelling photography records natural emotions, and studio sessions offer privacy and control over lighting and weather.

Each style involves trade-offs. Travelling overseas may produce striking pictures but costs more and takes time. Studio portraits are reliable but can look formal, while candid photographs may capture genuine feelings yet miss the carefully planned details of the ceremony. Family members may also have different ideas about what a wedding album should show.

A couple should decide whether the priority is personality, tradition, scenery or the relationships shared with guests. The best photographs may combine several approaches instead of following one fashion. Cost, comfort, privacy and the meaning the pictures will have many years later should all guide the choice for both partners involved.

replacement.title: Online Crime

context.source_line: Original practice article based on the verified 2019 HKDSE Paper 4 Set 1.3 scenario (not official text):
context.title: Online Crime: Questions and Trade-offs
body: Online scams can reach people through shopping sites, social media, dating platforms, email and text messages. A false seller may take payment without delivering the promised product, while a criminal may pretend to be a bank or a trusted friend in order to collect passwords, account details or money.

Students may believe they are unlikely targets because they have limited savings, but their identities, photographs and online accounts still have value. Reusing one password across several services makes a single mistake more serious. A friendly message can also create false trust before the sender asks for money or private information.

Protection begins with simple habits: use different passwords, turn on two-step verification, check web addresses and avoid rushed payments. Suspicious requests should be confirmed through another channel and reported to an adult, the platform or the police. Schools can help students practise recognising warning signs rather than merely telling them to be careful.

replacement.title: Fortune Telling

context.source_line: Original practice article based on the verified 2019 HKDSE Paper 4 Set 2.1 scenario (not official text):
context.title: Fortune Telling: Questions and Trade-offs
body: Fortune telling remains visible in parts of Hong Kong, especially around temples and traditional market streets. Visitors may have their palms or faces read, consult the Chinese zodiac or ask about relationships, careers and health. For some people the experience is entertainment; for others it is a serious cultural practice.

Its appeal comes partly from uncertainty. A confident prediction can make a person feel understood and may offer a way to organise difficult choices. Family customs and curiosity also attract customers. Critics, however, question whether vague statements only seem accurate and worry that vulnerable people may pay repeatedly for advice they cannot verify.

Modern technology may change the service rather than end it. Online readings can reach younger audiences, while traditional practitioners may continue to attract people who value face-to-face contact. Its future will depend on whether it is treated as cultural heritage, commercial entertainment or professional advice, and on how customers are protected from dishonest claims.

replacement.title: Apple Screen Time Control

context.source_line: Original practice article based on the verified 2019 HKDSE Paper 4 Set 2.2 scenario (not official text):
context.title: Apple Screen Time Control: Questions and Trade-offs
body: Screen-time tools allow parents to see how long children use particular apps and to set periods when games, videos or social media are unavailable. Essential services, such as school materials or emergency messages, can remain open. Supporters say these controls make family rules clear and reduce arguments about late-night phone use.

The software cannot solve every problem. A strict limit may interrupt useful work, and young people may feel that constant monitoring invades their privacy. They can also move to another device or focus on reaching the limit instead of learning self-control. Parents who spend hours on their own phones may find their rules difficult to defend.

Controls work best when families agree on the purpose of each rule and review it as children become more responsible. Device-free meals, sensible bedtimes and adults setting a good example can support the technology. The question is not only how much time students spend online, but what they do there and what offline activities are being displaced.

replacement.title: International Sport

context.source_line: Original practice article based on the verified 2019 HKDSE Paper 4 Set 2.3 scenario (not official text):
context.title: International Sport: Questions and Trade-offs
body: Small countries can succeed in international sport when they invest in facilities, qualified coaches and opportunities for young players. Iceland’s rise in football attracted attention because its population is limited, yet a long-term training system helped local athletes compete with much larger nations. Hong Kong faces similar limits on land and player numbers.

Sending coaches or youth teams overseas may expose them to new methods and a different sporting culture. Such exchanges can inspire athletes, but a short visit will not repair weak local leagues, limited school time or poor support for competitors. Money spent on officials and publicity may also be criticised if athletes lack medical or training resources.

Hong Kong must decide what success means: medals, public participation, healthier citizens or a stronger professional system. Learning from another country requires adapting its ideas rather than copying them. Schools, sports associations and government need clear responsibilities, patient funding and ways for talented young people to continue training.

replacement.title: Facebook

context.source_line: Original practice article based on the verified 2019 HKDSE Paper 4 Set 3.1 scenario (not official text):
context.title: Facebook: Questions and Trade-offs
body: Facebook once appeared to be the natural place for young people to share photographs, messages and news, but many users have moved to newer platforms. Older relatives, community groups and event organisers may still rely on it, so leaving completely can mean losing useful connections and information.

The service also raises questions about privacy and trust. Employers may look at public posts, false accounts can deceive users, and misleading stories may spread faster than corrections. A joke written for friends can remain searchable years later. People who compare their lives with carefully edited posts may also feel isolated rather than connected.

Users should review privacy settings, check the source of surprising claims and think before posting information about themselves or others. Social media is likely to remain popular even if individual brands rise and fall, because the desire to communicate will continue. The more important issue is whether future platforms give users meaningful control over their data and attention.

replacement.title: Sex Discrimination

context.source_line: Original practice article based on the verified 2019 HKDSE Paper 4 Set 3.2 scenario (not official text):
context.title: Sex Discrimination: Questions and Trade-offs
body: Pay differences between men and women cannot be explained simply by ability. Women and men can perform the same professional tasks, yet promotion decisions, occupational stereotypes and unequal caring responsibilities may shape their careers. A worker who takes time away to care for family members may lose experience, income and opportunities to advance.

Some employers assume that men are more suitable for competitive leadership or long working hours, while women are directed towards lower-paid caring and support roles. Even when the work is comparable, secrecy around salaries makes unfair differences hard to identify. These patterns can influence students before they enter the workplace.

Possible responses include transparent salary ranges, equal-pay reviews, affordable childcare and flexible arrangements available to all parents. Schools can challenge the idea that particular careers belong to one gender. Laws matter, but organisations must also examine how they recruit, evaluate and promote staff so that performance is judged by evidence rather than expectations.

replacement.title: Cheating

context.source_line: Original practice article based on the verified 2019 HKDSE Paper 4 Set 3.3 scenario (not official text):
context.title: Cheating: Questions and Trade-offs
body: When two homework assignments look almost identical, a school must find out what happened before deciding on a punishment. One student may have copied, both may have used the same online source, or they may have worked together when collaboration was not allowed. Similar work is a warning sign, not complete proof.

Students cheat for different reasons, including fear of failure, heavy workloads, unclear instructions and the belief that everyone else is doing it. Technology makes copied essays and automatic translation easy to obtain, but it can also help teachers compare drafts and understand how work developed. Punishment alone may hide the cause without changing behaviour.

A fair response should distinguish a first minor offence from repeated or organised dishonesty. Students need clear rules, a chance to explain and support if they lack skills or time management. Rewriting the task, meeting parents or detention may be appropriate, while serious cases require stronger action. Prevention should make honest work achievable as well as expected.

replacement.title: Living in a Densely Populated Urban Area

context.source_line: Original practice article based on the verified 2019 HKDSE Paper 4 Set 4.1 scenario (not official text):
context.title: Living in a Densely Populated Urban Area: Questions and Trade-offs
body: A small action in a crowded city can reveal very different ideas about courtesy. One lift passenger may hold the door for someone approaching, while another presses “close” because every second matters. The first person sees patience and consideration; the second sees an unnecessary delay for everyone already inside.

Similar conflicts occur on pavements, escalators, trains and in queues. Limited space and long working hours can make people hurried, but crowding does not excuse blocking doors, pushing or ignoring those who need a seat. At the same time, rules that sound polite may be impractical if they slow a busy system or create danger.

Better behaviour depends on clear expectations and awareness of other people. Signs, station announcements and school education can help, but design matters too: wider passages, visible queues and enough time for lift doors to close reduce conflict. Urban courtesy is not about performing one fixed gesture; it is about judging how an action affects others in that moment.

replacement.title: Unusual English Names

context.source_line: Original practice article based on the verified 2019 HKDSE Paper 4 Set 4.2 scenario (not official text):
context.title: Unusual English Names: Questions and Trade-offs
body: Many Hong Kong people use an English name at school or work. Some choose a familiar name because it is easy for teachers and colleagues to remember, while others select a word, brand or invented spelling that expresses individuality. A name may also resemble the sound or meaning of a person’s Chinese name.

Unusual names can be memorable and personally meaningful, but they may create unexpected problems. Listeners may not know how to pronounce them, computer forms may reject punctuation, and an employer may make unfair assumptions before meeting the applicant. A name that seems amusing to one culture may have an unwanted meaning in another.

Students should be free to decide how they wish to be addressed, yet it helps to check pronunciation, spelling and possible associations. They can use different names in informal and professional settings or simply use their Chinese name. Respect works both ways: the person choosing a name should consider its audience, and others should avoid mocking a choice they do not understand.

replacement.title: Person of the Year

context.source_line: Original practice article based on the verified 2019 HKDSE Paper 4 Set 4.3 scenario (not official text):
context.title: Person of the Year: Questions and Trade-offs
body: A school’s Person of the Year award can show students what kinds of achievement and behaviour the community values. Famous candidates may include artists, athletes, businesspeople or public officials, each representing a different route to success. Their stories can demonstrate perseverance, talent, service or the ability to overcome disadvantage.

Popularity alone is not a reliable standard. Students may know little about some nominees, disagree with their decisions or feel that celebrity receives more attention than quiet service. A person can also be successful without being a suitable role model in every part of life. The selection process should therefore explain which qualities are being recognised.

The school could invite nominations from students and require evidence of positive impact. Local volunteers, former students, teachers or young innovators may feel more relevant than internationally known figures. A balanced choice should inspire effort without suggesting that wealth or fame is the only measure of success, and should allow respectful disagreement about the final result.

context.source_line: Original practice article based on the verified 2019 HKDSE Paper 4 Set 5.1 scenario (not official text):
context.title: CCTV: Questions and Trade-offs
body: CCTV cameras can help a school investigate theft, bullying or damage and may discourage some unsafe behaviour. Recordings from entrances and public corridors can provide evidence when witnesses disagree. Parents may also feel reassured that incidents can be reviewed rather than decided only by rumour.

Constant recording, however, changes how a school feels. Cameras may capture private conversations, be placed where they are not necessary or create suspicion between students and staff. A recording can cause further harm if too many people can view it, if it is kept indefinitely or if it is used for a purpose students were never told about.

Any system needs rules before cameras are installed. The school should identify specific risks, avoid sensitive areas, limit access to authorised staff and delete recordings after a stated period unless an incident is being investigated. Students and parents should know where cameras are and how to complain. Security should be improved without treating everyone as a potential offender.

context.title: Space Travel: Questions and Trade-offs
body: Private companies have proposed sending wealthy passengers and invited artists around the Moon. Supporters say seeing Earth from space could inspire paintings, films and ideas that reach millions of people. Commercial missions may also test equipment, create jobs and reduce the cost of future launches without depending entirely on government programmes.

Space travel may become more common if safety improves and costs fall, but popularity should not be confused with public value. Clear goals and transparent costs are needed before calling it a good use of money.

context.source_line: Original practice article based on the verified 2019 HKDSE Paper 4 Set 6.1 scenario (not official text):
context.title: The Killing of Animals: Questions and Trade-offs
body: When wild animal numbers increase near homes, residents may report damaged property, stolen food or dangerous encounters. Governments sometimes use selective killing, or culling, to reduce a population quickly. Supporters argue that this protects people and prevents animals from starving when an area cannot support them.

Animal-welfare groups question whether culling addresses the cause. Feeding by visitors, easy access to rubbish and the loss of natural habitat can draw animals into urban areas. Relocating them may only move the conflict, while birth control is slower and needs long-term monitoring. No single method works equally well for every species or location.

A responsible programme should use reliable population data and consider non-lethal measures first. Secure bins, public education, enforcement against feeding and habitat management can reduce contact. If killing is proposed, authorities must explain why alternatives are insufficient and how suffering will be minimised. The debate requires both concern for human safety and respect for animal welfare.

context.source_line: Original practice article based on the verified 2019 HKDSE Paper 4 Set 6.2 scenario (not official text):
context.title: Translation Apps: Questions and Trade-offs
body: Translation devices can turn speech or writing into another language within seconds. Travellers may use them at hotels and restaurants, while students can check the general meaning of unfamiliar text or listen to pronunciation. They reduce anxiety when people need basic communication and no human interpreter is available.

A fluent-looking translation can still be wrong. Apps may miss humour, tone, technical meanings or cultural references, and users who do not know the target language may not notice the error. Schools need rules based on the purpose of a task. A device may be useful for research, accessibility or checking a draft, but not when the aim is to assess the student’s own language. Learning languages remains valuable for relationships, cultural understanding and judging whether technology is accurate. The strongest users will treat translation tools as assistance rather than a substitute for thought.

context.source_line: Original practice article based on the verified 2019 HKDSE Paper 4 Set 6.3 scenario (not official text):
context.title: Selfies: Questions and Trade-offs
body: Selfies make it easy to record an experience and share it immediately. A striking photograph can attract attention online, help friends feel connected and give travellers a personal memory. The search for an unusual background, however, can move attention away from what is happening around the photographer.

Accidents occur when people stand near cliffs, roads, trains, water or wild animals while concentrating on a screen. Social pressure may encourage a person to take greater risks for likes or to copy an image that appears safe online. Problems also include disturbing other visitors, revealing someone’s location and photographing people without permission.

Warnings and barriers are useful at known danger spots, but a complete ban may be difficult to enforce. Platforms, schools and tourist sites can explain how risky images are created and avoid rewarding dangerous behaviour. Before taking a photograph, users should stop, check the surroundings and decide whether the picture is worth the risk to themselves or anyone nearby.

body: Yuenyeung is a Hong Kong drink that combines coffee with milk tea and can be served hot or cold. Its Cantonese name refers to mandarin ducks, a traditional symbol of a pair. Local customers recognise it immediately, but visitors may not know how to pronounce the name or understand what the drink contains.

An English name could make menus and tourism advertising easier to understand. A simple description might explain the ingredients, while a creative name could be more memorable. Yet replacing the local name completely could remove the cultural story that makes the drink distinctive. A poor name might also suggest the wrong flavour or make it sound like an imported product.

Promotion could combine the original name with a clear explanation and consistent spelling. Cafés might offer tasting events, demonstrations or maps of traditional shops, while tourism campaigns could link the drink to Hong Kong’s café culture. The most suitable choice should be accurate, easy to say and strong enough to represent both the drink and its local identity.

context.title: Inequality in Hong Kong: Questions and Trade-offs
body: Hong Kong offers efficient transport, public services and opportunities in an international economy, yet residents do not share these benefits equally. High housing costs, different school resources and gaps between wages can shape where people live, what they can study and how secure they feel about the future.

Some inequality reflects different choices, skills and responsibilities, but very large gaps can reduce social mobility. Families with fewer resources may struggle to afford tutoring, suitable housing or time for training. When people believe that effort cannot improve their position, trust in institutions and other social groups may weaken.

Policies can address barriers without promising that every outcome will be identical. Affordable housing, accessible childcare, well-funded schools, job training and fair wages may widen opportunity. Taxes and benefits also require careful design so that help reaches those who need it without creating unnecessary complexity. A more equal society should be judged by dignity, opportunity and participation as well as income.

context.title: Co-living: Questions and Trade-offs
body: Co-living developments give residents a private sleeping area while kitchens, lounges, workspaces or laundry facilities are shared. Sharing expensive facilities may reduce costs and create opportunities to meet people in an unfamiliar city.

context.title: Age Limit for Political Leaders: Questions and Trade-offs
body: Political leadership requires judgement, communication, integrity and the ability to respond to change. Older leaders may offer long experience, knowledge of institutions and established relationships. Younger leaders may bring different priorities, greater familiarity with new technology and a longer personal stake in decisions about the future.

Age does not guarantee either wisdom or innovation. Health and energy vary greatly between individuals, and a young leader can be inflexible just as an older leader can adapt quickly. Voters and organisations should examine evidence of competence, health, ethics and recent performance rather than rely on a number alone. Term limits, transparent medical information and leadership teams with different generations may address some concerns more fairly. The goal is not to choose the youngest or oldest person, but to create accountable leadership that understands a changing society.

context.title: Can a Phone Teach Us When to Put It Down?
body: Most smartphones now show how much time users spend on different apps. They can block selected services after a daily limit, silence notifications during study periods and produce weekly reports. Supporters say the data turns an invisible habit into something measurable and helps families notice patterns that would otherwise be ignored.

Limits do not automatically create self-control. Users can press an “ignore” button, change settings or move to another device. Strict monitoring may damage trust and encourage secretive behaviour, especially when adults do not follow the same rules. The purpose of online activity also matters: an hour of homework is different from an hour of endless short videos.

Some families prefer a shared agreement in which everyone keeps phones away during meals, study sessions and before bedtime. Schools can teach students to manage notifications and recognise persuasive app design. Technology can provide reminders, but lasting change depends on motivation, realistic routines and honest conversations about sleep, learning and relationships.

replacement.title: Translation Apps and Language Learning

context.source_line: Original mock practice article (not an official HKDSE examination text):
context.title: A Helpful Language Partner — or a Dangerous Shortcut?
body: Translation apps are fast, inexpensive and easy to use. A traveller can point a phone camera at a menu, while a student can listen to the pronunciation of an unfamiliar phrase. The apps reduce anxiety and may help people communicate in an emergency when no interpreter is available.

A smooth translation can still be misleading. Software may miss humour, cultural references, specialist meanings and the speaker’s tone. Students who paste an entire assignment into an app may submit unnatural sentences without understanding the grammar. Constant dependence can also prevent learners from thinking directly in the language they are studying.

Used carefully, an app can act as a dictionary, pronunciation guide and checking tool. Students should compare uncertain results, declare when substantial help was used and keep a record of their own corrections. Schools need rules that distinguish learning support from work that falsely appears to be the student’s own language.
